bib.title: Appendix C: Building knowledge graphs from structured sources (in Knowledge Graphs and LLMs in Action)
authors: Negro et al. (book authors; chapter text prints none)

question: How do you build a knowledge graph for miRNA-disease association prediction from existing structured data sources, normalize its entities and check the result?
contributions: Step-by-step build of a miRNA KG from HMDD, dbDEMC, miR2Disease, miRBase, miRDB and MISIM with Neo4j importers
Disease normalization to UMLS via scispaCy, kept as separate NormalizedDisease nodes
Evaluation of normalization with WCC and all-pairs shortest paths
Exploration with weighted node similarity and degree-weighted path count

results.claim: The chapter argues shorter miRNA-miRNA connections give higher-quality final embeddings, but runs no link prediction before and after normalization to test it.

limits: Prediction (link prediction) models are not covered; only construction and exploration.
Normalization benefit is argued via shorter paths, not measured by a downstream model.
WCC showed no significant change after normalization because the graph was already one giant component.
Celiac-disease literature check found support for only some top targets; others had no easy-to-access articles.
LLM-based entity normalization is discussed as an alternative but not run; named limits are non-reproducible output and compute cost.
APSP was in the alpha tier of Neo4j GDS at the time of writing; gds.graph.project.cypher and CREATE CONSTRAINT ON ... ASSERT syntax are dated.
practices: Do not ingest every available dataset; select datasets that serve the task, because each adds noise and reconciliation errors (C.2).
Use the first low-complexity KG as a baseline to quantify what later sources add (C.2).
Keep one relationship type per source (RELATED_TO, REGULATES) to preserve nuances and provenance (C.2.1).
Use MERGE on a name key so datasets fuse into a single node per entity (C.2.1).
Normalize disease names against UMLS, but add NormalizedDisease nodes instead of merging, so results can be reviewed and reset (C.2.2).
Evaluate normalization by comparing WCC and shortest-path distributions before and after (C.2.2).
Use gds.graph.project for speed and Cypher projections for exploration and debugging (C.2.2).
Check database size and contents with simple exercises before running algorithms (C.2.3).
Use DWPC to penalize highly connected nodes when ranking disease-target paths (C.3).
